items.demo: Try it: kill the data provider

problem.plain: Company trees 20–30 levels deep took minutes to load and often failed. The database couldn't be changed.
problem.tech: Hierarchies 20–30 levels deep, up to 30 children per node, in RDS. Recursive assembly in Lambda took 3–4 min and timed out. NoSQL was not an option.

did.plain: Built a ready-made copy of the tree that updates itself every time something changes.
did.tech: Precomputed hierarchy JSON in S3, rebuilt by a sync Lambda on every change through SQS (latest wins). Reads skip RDS entirely.

changed.plain: Pages now load the tree instantly.
changed.tech: No recursion on the read path, and the Lambda timeouts are gone.

diagram.aria: Company edit → SQS → sync Lambda → S3 tree.json → read Lambda → UI. Before: UI → Lambda → recursive database joins, 3–4 min, timeout.
diagram.before: before: UI → Lambda → recursive DB joins · 3–4 min · timeout

problem.plain: A live donations platform had to move to a new system with no downtime, no lost records, no access to payment details, and a daily 5 AM charge run that could never be missed.
problem.tech: Live recurring-payments platform moving to a new Postgres-based backend and auth provider. No production access (payment tokens in the DB), a CMS schema that could not be exported directly, and a daily 5 AM charge cron.

did.plain: Planned and rehearsed every step on a test copy first, and led the team as manager, developer and client contact.
did.tech: Extraction scripts through the CMS API, covering referenced modules, media and tokens, rehearsed on staging. Auth migrated; the cron guarded through cutover.

changed.plain: The move went smoothly. Donors never noticed, and the team earned a bonus.
changed.tech: 0 downtime, 0 data loss, 0 tokens exposed, 0 missed charge runs. Team bonus.

diagram.aria: Old backend and auth → migration scripts rehearsed on staging → new Postgres platform with new auth; the daily 5 AM charge run never missed.

playertotals.title: PlayerTotals: live sports stats

problem.plain: The client wanted fast, recent NBA, NFL and MLB stats, and the data supplier limits how often you can ask.
problem.tech: External stats APIs with hard rate limits, and a requirement for near-real-time stats across three leagues.

did.plain: Fetch on a schedule, keep the newest stats in fast memory, and keep our own copy of the history.
did.tech: Cron ingestion every 5 minutes into MongoDB (versioned, keeps history); a Redis hot window with bounded memory and instance count.

changed.plain: Stats load fast, are at most 2–3 minutes old, and old stats survive even if the supplier drops them.
changed.tech: Data at most 2–3 min old, upstream rate limits respected, history independent of the provider.

diagram.aria: Stats APIs → cron jobs every 5 minutes → Redis hot window and MongoDB full history → fans.
